t: Gandhi launched the movement in Bombay on 8 August 1942 with a call to Do or Die, after the Cripps Mission failed to win Indian support for the war effort, and almost the whole Congress leadership was in prison within hours.

Without its leaders the movement took the form of strikes, boycotts, sabotage and local parallel governments, and the British answered with more than 100,000 arrests, mass fines, public flogging and the killing of hundreds of civilians.
The Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha, the Communist Party of India and some princes opposed the movement, while Viceroy Linlithgow called it by far the most serious rebellion since 1857.
dyk: Viceroy Linlithgow told Winston Churchill in a telegram of 31 August 1942 that the gravity and extent of the rebellion had been concealed from the world for reasons of military security.
ev: India is brought into the war without consultation, and the Congress ministers of eight provinces resign
The Cripps Mission fails to win Congress support, and Gandhi calls its offer a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank
The Congress working committee at Wardha adopts a resolution demanding complete independence on 14 July
Gandhi delivers his Quit India speech at Bombay on 8 August, and almost the entire Congress leadership is imprisoned within hours
Between 9 August and 21 September protesters attack post offices, railway stations and police stations, and 57 battalions of British troops are deployed
Gandhi is released on account of his health and demands the release of the Congress leadership
All jailed nationalists are released after the Labour Party wins the British election

f.where: British India, with the strongest local effects at Satara in Maharashtra, Talcher in Odisha, Midnapore in Bengal, Ballia in what is now Uttar Pradesh, parts of Saurashtra in Gujarat and, with the greatest violence, Bihar
f.period: Congress working committee resolution at Wardha on 14 July 1942; launch at Bombay on 8 August 1942; mass arrests and local risings from August to September 1942; underground resistance and parallel governments, with leaders in prison, until 1945; release of all jailed nationalists in 1945
f.figures: Mohandas Gandhi, who called on the people to Do or Die; Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Azad, who were apprehensive but backed the call; Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad, who supported it openly; Aruna Asaf Ali, who presided over the All India Congress Committee session on 9 August; Jayaprakash Narayan and Asoka Mehta; underground leaders such as Achyut Rao Patwardhan, Sucheta Kripalani and Nana Patil
f.outcome: almost all of the Congress leadership was imprisoned, more than 100,000 people were arrested and hundreds of civilians were killed; the movement ended in 1945 with the release of the jailed nationalists, after Labour won the British election promising independence for India
